Area.evidence_source: The current study's findings reveal social isolation as a complex construct demanding attention to an array of contributing and oftentimes interconnected dynamics. For example, estrangement from family emerged early on for many men, setting the tone for additional "othering" experiences at school and work. For many men, this lack of belonging experienced early in life fueled isolating tendencies and detachment from health services and effective self-care amid compounding dislocating thoughts. This cascade of isolating influences ultimately rendered the men burdensome and immoral subjects, society's outsiders who endured multiple stigmas away from judging eyes and/or by contemplating relief through suicide. This is not to espouse a domino effect model wherein isolation was forged incrementally and chronologically for every participant (though that was the case for many men). Some men experienced mental illness and suicidality later in life, as responses to emergent challenges petitioning cognitive and emotional disidentity brought on by significant acute social changes (i.e., unemployment) and structural challenges for soliciting effective help. In this regard, the six themes describing men's social isolation might be understood as diverse in their attribution; yet individually and/or collectively they proved potent drivers.
